Effect of salinity on diazotrophic activity and microbial composition of phototrophic communities from Bitter-1 soda lake (Kulunda Steppe, Russia) Zorigto Namsaraev1 · Olga Samylina2 · Marina Sukhacheva3 · Gennadii Borisenko4 · Dimitry Y. Sorokin2,5 · Tatiana Tourova2 Received: 26 February 2018 / Accepted: 6 April 2018 / Published online: 16 April 2018 © Springer Japan KK, part of Springer Nature 2018 Abstract Bitter-1 is a shallow hypersaline soda lake in Kulunda Steppe (Altai region, Russia). During a study period between 2005 and 2016, the salinity in the littoral area of the lake fluctuated within the range from 85 to 400 g/L (in July of each year). Light-dependent nitrogen fixation occurred in this lake up to the salt-saturating conditions. The rates increased with a decrease in salinity, both under environmental conditions and in laboratory simulations. The salinities below 100 g/L were favorable for light-dependent nitrogen fixation, while the process was dramatically inhibited above 200 g/L salts. The analysis of nifH genes in environmental samples and in enrichment cultures of diazotrophic phototrophs suggested that anaerobic fermenting and sulfate-reducing bacteria could participate in the dark nitrogen fixation process up to soda-saturating conditions. However, we cannot exclude the possibility that haloalkaliphilic nonheterocystous cyanobacteria (Euhalothece sp. and Geitlerinema sp.) and anoxygenic purple sulfur bacteria (Ectothiorhodospira sp.) might also play a role in the process at light conditions. The heterocystous cyanobacterium Nodularia sp. develops at low salinity (below 80 g/L) that is not characteristic for Bitter-1 Lake and thus does not make a significant contribution to the nitrogen fixation in this lake. Keywords Nitrogen fixation · Phototrophic bacteria · Sulfate-reducing bacteria · Hypersaline · Soda lakes Introduction The equatorial soda lakes are considered to be the most productive types of an ecosystem on the Earth showing primary production rates in excess of 10 g/(m² day) (Grant 2006; Melack 1981). The primary production of organic matter in the soda lakes of the cryoarid climate during summer time is not so high and is up to 3.86 g/(m² day) according to Namsaraev et al. (2015). Nitrogen availability is one of the most important limiting factors for primary production (Axler et al. 1978). Detection of high concentrations of ammonium in many soda lakes, which easily escapes to atmosphere at high pH (Jellison et al. 1993), as well as the functioning of nitrifying/denitrifying bacteria (Sorokin and Kuenen 2005; Boltyanskaya et al. 2007; Shapovalova et al. 2008) indicates the operation of an active nitrogen cycle in these extreme ecosystems. Moderately haloalkaliphilic heterocystous cyanobacteria capable of fixing nitrogen under aerobic light conditions are abundant in soda lakes at salt concentrations below 70 g/L. Various species of Anabaenopsis, Cyanospira, and Nodularia are abundant in the plankton of the moderately saline soda lakes of the East African Rift and South Siberia (Krienitz and Schagerl 2016; Tsyrenova et al. 2011), while a dominance of heterocystous cyanobacteria (primarily Anabaenopsis spp.) in shallow soda lakes of the Kulunda Steppe (Southern Siberia, Russia) was noted as early as in the 1920s–1930s at salinities up to 50 g/L (Voronikhin 1929; Isachenko 1934). At the salinities higher than 70 g/L, the heterocystous cyanobacteria are not usually detected (Oren 2011a). At these conditions, the diazotrophic bacteria are represented by heterotrophic microaerobes and anaerobes (Sorokin et al. 2014a, b, 2015a; Sorokin 2017). A study of the nifH gene diversity in the highly mineralized lakes of the Kulunda steppe and the Wadi Natrun (Egypt) showed the presence of genes belonging to representatives of various phyla, including anoxygenic purple sulfur and nonsulfur proteobacteria, green nonsulfur bacteria, heliobacteria, and oxygenic cyanobacteria, as well as anaerobic heterotrophic bacteria (Tourova et al. 2014). The activity of light-stimulated and light-independent nitrogen fixation in aerobic and anaerobic conditions was detected at salinity 90–100 g/L in bottom sediments and floating phototrophic biomass in the alkaline Mono Lake (USA) (Oremland 1990; Herbst 1998). Further increase of salinity inhibited the activity of light-dependent fixation of nitrogen in Mono Lake (Herbst 1998). Yet, it is still unclear which groups of prokaryotes are responsible for nitrogen fixation in hypersaline alkaline lakes, including lakes of Kulunda Steppe. Unlike bigger and more stable Mono Lake, the shallow Kulunda lakes have significant annual fluctuations of salinity. We assumed that the haloalkaliphilic microbial communities in the Kulunda Steppe lakes should be diazotrophically active in a wide range of salinity to support the functioning of a nitrogen cycle. To test this hypothesis, we studied a hypersaline soda lake Bitter-1 located in the southern part of the Kulunda Steppe (Altai region, Russia). During the period of our studies (2005–2016), the total salt concentration of the lake brines fluctuated between 85 and 400 g/L, the total soluble alkalinity from 1 to 4 M, and the pH from 9.6 to 10.5 (all measurements were made in July of each year). It gave us an opportunity to study the influence of salinity on the in situ nitrogen-fixing activity and the composition of diazotrophic phototrophic communities developing in this unique hypersaline and hyperalkaline habitat. Materials and methods Study site Lake Bitter-1 belongs to the Mikhailovsky group of soda lakes located 20 km east of the Russian-Kazakhstan border in the Kulunda Steppe (Altai Region, south-western Siberia, Russia) (Fig. 1). It has the following coordinates: 51°40′19.1″N 79°54′20.4″E. Four small shallow soda lakes under the general name of Bitter (or “Gorchiny” in Russian pronunciation) are located about 7 km to the east from the village of Malinovoe Ozero and Tanatar soda lake system and 4 km to the north from the freshwater lake Demkino. The Bitter lake system is formed in a drainless trona-cemented sand basin and surrounded by a pine forest. During the period of our studies, the Bitter-1 and Bitter-3 were lakes with soda brines, Bitter-2 was a dry soda pan, and Bitter-4 was a hyposaline soda lake. The microbiological study of these lakes have started in 2003 (Foti et al. 2007, 2008; Sorokin et al. 2008a, b, 2014a, b, 2015a; Kompantseva et al. 2010; Samylina et al. 2014; Tourova et al. 2014). Earlier research is not known to us; however, it was exploited by the local residents, since the 1940s as a trona mineral resource. Samples of the surface layer of sediments, microbial mats, and overlaying brines were collected from the littoral area of the Bitter-1 lake. The depth of the lake was less than 15 cm at the sampling site. Acetylene-reduction activity assays were conducted upon collection in the field and, in addition, in the laboratory experiments with different salinities. All collected samples were stored at ambient temperature until their analysis in the laboratory (max. storage time—5 days). Salinity and pH of the brines were measured using a WTW field potentiometer–conductometer. For the hypersaline conditions, the average pH values between the native brine and its 1:5 dilution was used. The total salinity values were additionally verified gravimetrically in the laboratory after the brine filtration through syringe 0.45 μm filters, and the average of the values obtained by the two methods was used. The soluble carbonate alkalinity was determined in the field by a two-step titration with 1 M HCl: (1) down to pH 8.0 (carbonate alkalinity) and (2) further down to pH 4.0 (the bicarbonate formed from carbonate + native bicarbonate alkalinity) (Reznikov et al. 1970). Chlorophyll a concentration in samples was analyzed spectrophotometrically according to Namsaraev (2009). The images were obtained using the AxioVision Rel. 4.7 software package. C₂H₂ reduction assay The C₂H₂ reduction assay for potential nitrogenase activity was conducted according to Hardy et al. (1968). For this, 5 cm³ of phototrophic biomass slurry in the native brines (to maintain the natural density of biomass) was added in a 25 mL flask stoppered with gray rubber and flushed with argon gas and 15% v/v final concentration of C₂H₂ was added to the head space and incubated for 1, 3, 6, or 24 h. Dark-incubated samples were wrapped in two layers of aluminium foil. To some of the incubations, sulfide was added at concentration of 1 mg/L. 0.5 mL gas samples were taken for analysis of C₂H₄ by a Chromatek Krystall 5000.1 gas chromatograph with a flame ionization detector as a measure of nitrogenase activity. To investigate the influence of salinity on nitrogenase activity, we used both the analysis of acetylene-reduction rates in the environmental samples collected during several seasons (data in Table 1; Fig. 3a) and the results of the laboratory experiment with a dilution of the environmental sample collected in 2014 with a salinity 200 g/L (data presented in Fig. 3b). We diluted it with distilled water down to 100 and 50 g/L. The samples were left overnight at low light intensity for adaptation of the microbial community to the decreased salinity levels before addition of C₂H₂ in the laboratory experiment. Incubation time was 72 h at 22 °C and a light intensity 100 μmol/m² s. Results were obtained from two biological replicates. All results are presented as means ± range of values. Enrichment cultures The enrichment cultures of haloalkaliphilic phototrophic bacteria were obtained using the Zarrouk medium (Vonshak 1997) (total salt concentration 22 g/L) with additional NaCl resulting in the salinity levels of 80, 150, and 200 g/L, respectively, and were incubated under aerobic conditions. At the salinity of 200 g/L, the second type of medium was also used. It contained an inhibitor of oxygenic photosynthesis DCMU (3-(3,4-dichlorophenyl)-1,1-dimethylurea) at a concentration of 7 μM, 0.5 g/L NH₄Cl, 0.5 g/L KH₂PO₄, 0.2 g/L MgCl₂, 18 g/L NaHCO₃, 180 g/L NaCl, 0.1 g/L yeast extract, 0.5 g/L sodium acetate, 0.5 g/L Na₂S·9H₂O, and 0.5 g/L Na₂S₂O₃·5H₂O, and were incubated anaerobically under N₂. For each type of medium, two versions of media were prepared: with nitrogen and without nitrogen source. In the aerobic variants with nitrogen at salinities of 22, 80, 150, and 200 g/L, 2.5 g/L sodium nitrate was used; in the anaerobic variant with a salinity of 200 g/L, 0.5 g/L ammonium chloride was used. Samples of surface layers of the sediments collected from the littoral area of the Bitter-1 lake in 2011 and 2012 were added at 5% v/v concentration.

Isolation of cyanobacterial cultures The cyanobacterial culture Nodularia sp. 10KLT1 was isolated in 2008 from Tanatar 1 soda lake sample using solid Zarrouk medium without sodium nitrate (Rippka 1988; Vonshak 1997). The cyanobacterial cultures Geitlerinema sp. T6-1124, Nodosilinea sp. T6-1119, and Euhalothece sp. T2-1114 were isolated in 2011 from samples of phototrophic biomass collected in Tanatar 2 and Tanatar 6 soda lakes. The enrichment cultures were obtained at three different salt combinations: 4 M Na\(^+\) (1.3 M NaHCO\(_3\) + Na\(_2\)CO\(_3\), pH 9.7), 2 M Na\(^+\) (0.58 M NaHCO\(_3\) + Na\(_2\)CO\(_3\), pH 10.2), and 0.75 M Na\(^+\) (0.2 M NaHCO\(_3\) + Na\(_2\)CO\(_3\), pH 9). The filamentous cyanobacteria Geitlerinema sp. T6-1124 and Nodosilinea sp. T6-1119 dominated in the media with 2 M and 0.75 M Na\(^+\), while the unicellular Euhalothece sp. T2-1114—in the 4 M Na\(^+\) medium, but it was also obtained in 2 M Na\(^+\) medium after prolong incubation. The isolation of strains from enrichment cultures was performed on solid media of the same composition. Nodosilinea sp. T6-1119 was maintained in the medium “S” with the following composition (g/L): NaHCO\(_3\)—16.8, NaCl—30.0, KCl—1.0, K\(_2\)HPO\(_4\)·3H\(_2\)O—0.5, NaNO\(_3\)—2.5, K\(_2\)SO\(_4\)—1.0, MgSO\(_4\)·7H\(_2\)O—0.1, CaCl\(_2\)—0.04, FeSO\(_4\)—0.01, EDTA—0.08, trace elements solution (TES) A5—1 mL/L, pH 9.0–9.5. Geitlerinema sp. T6-1124, and Euhalothece sp. T2-1114 were maintained in the medium “M” with the following composition (g/L): Na\(_2\)CO\(_3\)—79.5, NaHCO\(_3\)—21.0, KCl—2.0, K\(_2\)HPO\(_4\)·3H\(_2\)O—0.5, KNO\(_3\)—2.0, Na\(_2\)SO\(_4\)—1.4, FeCl\(_3\)—0.0003, EDTA—0.0005, TES A5—1 mL/L, pH 10.0. The composition of TES A5 is (g/L): H\(_3\)BO\(_3\)—2.86, MgCl\(_2\)·4H2O—1.81, ZnSO\(_4\)·7H\(_2\)O—0.222, Na\(_2\)MoO\(_4\)·2H\(_2\)O—0.39, CuSO\(_4\)·5H\(_2\)O—0.079, and Co(NO\(_3\))\(_2\)·6H\(_2\)O—0.0494. All cultures were incubated at room temperature and natural light–dark cycles. The identification of the cultures and microscopic analysis of environmental samples were performed according to Samylina et al. (2014). DNA isolation DNA isolation from sediments of Bitter-1 Lake was carried out with the MoBio Power Soil DNA Isolation kit (MoBio Laboratories). Approximately 10 g of sediment was washed from alkalinity with 1 M NaCl; the suspension was centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 2 min to remove the coarse fraction, and the remaining fine colloidal fraction was centrifuged further 2–3 times at 5000 rpm, depending on the sediment type. From the colloidal suspension thus obtained, a 22 mL portion was finally collected at maximum speed and used for DNA isolation after adjusting the pH to 7.5 with 0.5 M HCl. Amplification, cloning, and sequencing For amplification and sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene, the universal bacterial primers were used (Edwards et al. 1989). For amplification and sequencing of the nifH and cbbL genes, we used primers and protocols described earlier (Marusina et al. 2001; Spiridonova et al. 2004; Tourova et al. 2010). PCR fragments of the expected size were excised from the gel, purified using the Wizard PCR Preps kit (Promega, United States), and sequenced immediately (for pure cultures) or after cloning (for soda lake sediment samples and enrichment cultures). Cloning was performed using the CloneJet PCR Cloning kit (Fermentas) including plasmid pJET1.2/blunt according to the manufacturer’s protocol. From each clone library, 20–50 clones were tested for the presence of the insert by PCR with specific primers. Clones containing the target insert were sequenced. Sequencing of amplification products and obtained clones was performed according to Sanger, using the Big Dye Terminator v.3.1 kit on an automatic ABI 3730 sequencer (Applied Biosystems Inc., United States), according to the instructions of the manufacturer. Phylogenetic analysis The sequences were edited with the use of BioEdit (http://jwbrown.mbio.ncsu.edu/BioEdit/bioediTca.html). Primary comparison of the de novo determined sequences with sequences available in the GenBank database was performed by using BLAST at the NCBI site (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/blast). For further comparative analysis 16S rRNA, nifH and cbbL genes sequences were retrieved from GenBank. Nucleotide sequences of the genes studied and amino acid sequences deduced were aligned with relevant sequences of the closest bacterial species with the use of CLUSTALX 2.0 (http://bips.uustrasbg.fr/fr/Documentation/ClustalX/). Phylogenetic trees were constructed using the TREECONW (http://bioccwww.uia.ac.be/u/yvdp/treeconw.html) and MEGA 6.0 (http://www.megasoftware.net/) software packages. The statistical significance of the branching order was determined by bootstrap analysis of 1000 alternative trees and expressed in percent. The nucleotide sequences of the 16S rRNA, nifH, and cbbL genes determined in this work were deposited in GenBank with accession numbers MG197455- MG197477. Results Phototrophic community of the Bitter-1 soda lake Bitter-1 soda lake has stable alkaline conditions with pH values of 9.6–10.5 due to its extremely high soluble carbonate alkalinity (Table 1). The fluctuations in salinity had a long interannual cycle with periods of relatively “high” and “low” salinity. The separation into periods was done by us depending on the type of phototrophic community that developed in the lake. During 11 years of observation, the change of such periods occurred twice. In 2005–2007, a period of relatively low salinity below 200 g/L was observed, followed by a hypersaline period of 2008–2012 (300–400 g/L), and in 2013–2016, the low salinity period (85–200 g/L) has started again. At the low salinity periods, the lake water was dominated by a loose biomass of a filamentous green alga Ctenocladus circinnatus or ephemeral cyanobacterial films (the same as described in Samylina et al. (2014). Potentially diazotrophic phototrophic prokaryotes in these types of communities were represented by haloalkaliphilic cyanobacteria Geitlerinema sp., Nodosilinea sp., Euhalothece sp., and anoxygenic purple sulfur bacteria of the genus Ectothiorhodospira (Fig. 2). The high salinity period was characterized by the endoevaporite phototrophic communities, which developed between the trona crystals under the salt crust. Potential diazotrophs, in this case, were extremely salt-tolerant unicellular cyanobacteria Euhalothece sp. and purple sulfur bacteria of the genera Halorhodospira and Ectothiorhodospira. The heterocystous cyanobacteria were not observed in the lake. Acetylene reduction by phototrophic communities At the period of high salinity from 2008 to 2012, phototrophic communities did not form mats on the surface of sediments, but developed among the crystals within the trona crust forming on the surface of sediments. This was collected to measure the acetylene-reduction activity. The acetylene-reduction activity was not detected in the sample collected in 2008 at salinity of 400 g/L (Table 1). However, in the 2011–2012 samples with total salt concentrations of 350–400 g/L a low, but detectable, level of acetylene reduction was observed (Fig. 3a). The addition of sulfide to the 2012 samples inhibited the light-dependent activity 4.8-fold (from 0.58 ± 0.08 to 0.12 ± 0.11 nmol C2H4/mL h). In contrast, sulfide did not influence the light-independent activity which maximum level was 0.18 ± 0.08 nmol C2H4/(mL h). The decrease of the lake’s salinity started in 2013 favored the formation of biofilms of the filamentous cyanobacteria on the bottom of the lake which diazotrophic potential was tested in 2014 at a salinity of 200 g/L. The rates of acetylene reduction were comparable to those measured at a higher salinity, and the light-dependent acetylene reduction exceeded the activity in the dark. Further decrease in salinity in 2016 down to a minimal 85 g/L caused a mass development of green algae and cyanobacteria that exhibited a much higher diazotrophic potential (Table 1). A simulated decrease in salinity in a laboratory experiment with the samples collected in 2014 and diluted from 200 g/L to 100 and 50 g/L also stimulated nitrogen fixation. On the third day of the light incubation, the growth of cyanobacteria and anoxygenic purple bacteria on the bottom and walls of vials was observed accompanied with a statistically significant increase in the ethylene concentration in the salt-diluted variants (Fig. 3b). In contrast, the decrease in salinity did not stimulate nitrogen fixation in the dark incubations. The rates of acetylene reduction observed in this experiment cannot represent the in situ rates because of the prolonged incubation (3 days) and the obvious growth of phototrophic bacteria, but it certainly confirms data obtained with environmental samples. Analysis of nifH and cbbL genes in the reference cultures of haloalkaliphilic cyanobacteria In earlier studies of the Kulunda Steppe soda lakes, the nifH and cbbL gene sequences of haloalkaliphilic cyanobacteria isolated from those lakes were not available. Therefore, for a more accurate identification of these organisms in environmental samples and enrichment cultures, we isolated four cultures of haloalkaliphilic cyanobacteria. Based on the morphological features and analysis of the 16S rRNA gene, these cultures were assigned to the genera Geitlerinema, Nodosilinea, Euhalothece, and Nodularia. Amplification products with primers for nifH genes F1-R6 (Marusina et al. 2001) were obtained for all studied strains. Amplification with the primers for cbbL genes cbbLG1f-cbbL1106r (Tourova et al. 2010) was successful for strains Geitlerinema sp. T6-1124 and Nodosilinea sp. T6-1119. For Euhalothece sp. T2-1114, only the primers RubIgF–RubIgR (Spiridonova et al. 2004) were efficient. For Nodularia sp 10KLT1, amplification was unsuccessful with all primer pares used. The position of the studied strains is shown in the phylogenetic trees (Figs. 4, 5, 6). In general, the functional gene phylogeny was consistent with the ribosomal gene phylogeny, with one exception. The T6-1124 culture according to analysis of the 16S rRNA and the cbbL genes belonged to the genus of Geitlerinema, while sequence of the nifH gene of this organism belonged to the cluster of Deltaproteobacteria. There, it formed a subcluster including sequences of the nifH gene from Geitlerinema (former Microcoleus) sp. Diversity of nifH genes in hypersaline soda lake Bitter-1 From the environmental samples of the surface layers of the sediments collected in Bitter-1 soda lake in 2011 and 2012 (at the salinity level of 350 and 400 g/L, respectively), the clone libraries were created using primers specific for nifH genes. The libraries with 43 and 47 clones contained 2 unique nifH phylotypes, pairwise identical in both libraries (Fig. 5). The dominant phylotypes in both libraries (34 and 39 clones) formed a separate subcluster within the cluster of sulfate-reducing Deltaproteobacteria. This phylotype was not identical to the Geitlerinema sp. T6-1124 that also possessed the nifH gene related to Deltaproteobacteria. The second phylotype found in environmental samples was distantly related to members of Clostridia. Thus, in the diazotrophic community of environmental samples collected during the salt-saturated period, the phototrophic diazotrophs, including cyanobacteria, were undetectable. Enrichment cultures of phototrophic microorganisms We tried to model the changes of salinity in the lake and obtained the enrichment cultures of phototrophic microorganisms at different salinities on media without combined nitrogen, as well as on media with the introduction of nitrogen compounds (NaNO3 or NH4Cl). We used surface layers of the sediments collected in 2011 and 2012 as inoculum for this experiment. An overview of the variants of enrichment cultures is presented in Table 2. In the absence of nitrogen sources, a stable growth was observed only in two variants: first, at low levels of salinity (22 g/L) and aerobic conditions, in which filamentous heterocystous cyanobacterium Nodularia sp. dominated in the sample; second, at high salinity (200 g/L) and anaerobic conditions (gas phase with N2), in which extremely halotolerant anoxogenic phototrophic bacteria of the genus Ectothiorhodospira were the dominant diazotrophs. At the salinity of 200 g/L, aerobic conditions, and absence of combined nitrogen, steady growth of microorganisms was not observed except a weak initial development of Picocystis salinarum (previously identified as Chlorella minutissima; Gerasimenko et al. 1999), and at the salinity of 80–150 g/L—of the unicellular microalgae Dunaliella sp., Picocystis salinarum (Fig. 2) and filamentous cyanobacterium Geitlerinema sp., probably due to the traces of combined nitrogen introduced into the medium with the inoculum. In the presence of combined nitrogen, growth was observed at all salinity values. At 22 and 80 g/L, the unicellular microalgae Dunaliella sp., Picocystis salinarum, and filamentous cyanobacterium Geitlerinema sp. were dominating the cultures. At salinity of 150 g/L, the filamentous cyanobacterium Geitlerinema sp. was replaced by the unicellular cyanobacterium Euhalothecae sp. capable of growth at salt-saturating conditions (Garcia-Pichel et al. 1998; Mikhodyuk et al. 2008). At salinity of 200 g/L in the aerobic conditions, the weak growth of Picocystis salinarum was observed. In the anaerobic light conditions and salinity of 200 g/L with combined nitrogen, the purple anoxogenic bacteria of the genus Ectothiorhodospira were dominant. Thus, despite the absence of phototrophic nifH sequences in the clone libraries obtained from the sediments at salinity 350–400 g/L, several groups of phototrophic diazotrophic microorganisms were present in sediments. These are filamentous heterocystous cyanobacteria Nodularia sp. and the anoxogenic phototrophic bacteria of the genus Ectothiorhodospira. A clone library 12G1-80 (30 clones) included 2 phylotypes. The dominant phylotype (27 clones) was identical to the nifH gene of the alkaliphilic cyanobacterium Geitlerinema sp. T6-1124, and a minor one—to the alkaliphilic cyanobacterium Euhalothece sp. T2-1114 and nifH phylotypes found in the samples from Bitter-1 lake collected in 2009 (Tourova et al. 2014). The clone library 11G1-150 (17 clones) contained a single phylotype also identical to Euhalothece sp. T2-1114. The clone library from the anaerobic enrichment culture 12G1-200 (21 clones) contained a single phylotype, closely related to the nifH gene of the purple sulfur bacterium Ectothiorhodospira haloalkaliphila. In an additional analysis using specific primers cbbLG1f-cbbL1106r for the detection of cbbL genes, the amplification product was detected in three cultures out of four (except 11G1-150) (Fig. 6). Each clone library contained only a single cbbL phylotype. A clone library 12G1-23 (25 clones) was most similar to the cbbL gene of the green nonsulfur bacterium Oscillochloris trichoides DG-6, a clone library 12G1-80 (30 clones)—to the cbbL gene of the haloalkaliphilic cyanobacterium Geitlerinema sp. T6-1124, and the library 12G1-200 (15 clones)—to a cbbL gene sequence of a gammaproteobacterium, most probably a member of Ectothiorhodospira. These data, in general, do not contradict the data obtained during analysis of nifH genes in the same cultures.  Discussion At the salinity level below 70 g/L, heterocystous cyanobacteria are one of the dominant groups of diazotrophic phototrophs in soda lakes (Oren 2011a). Due to the presence of heterocysts, protecting nitrogenase from the oxidative stress, these cyanobacteria are capable of fixing nitrogen in fully aerobic environment. As a result, the rate of light-dependent nitrogen fixation significantly exceeds the fixation in the dark as was shown by Oremland (1983) during a study of Big Soda Lake. At hypersaline conditions above 70 g/L, the situation becomes more complicated. The heterocystous cyanobacteria become inactive, but oxygenic photosynthesis still occurs (Namsaraev et al. 2015). Which groups of bacteria are capable of fixing nitrogen under these conditions remained unclear. In addition to the formation of heterocysts, the phototrophic microorganisms have various mechanisms of nitrogen fixation in the presence of oxygen (Berman-Frank et al. 2003). First, some cyanobacteria, for example, Plectonema boryanum, are capable of nitrogen fixation under microaerobic conditions with an oxygen content of less than 1.5% in the dark and less than 0.5% in the light. Second, temporal separation is possible, when nitrogen fixation occurs at night and oxygenic photosynthesis during the day time. Third, a combination of these strategies is possible, as in the marine nonheterocystous filamentous cyanobacterium Trichodesmium, in which a part of the cells in the cyanobacterial trichome (up to 10–20% of the total number of cells) can fix nitrogen, and the ability to achieve nitrogen can be activated when necessary. The diversity of these strategies in cultures isolated from hypersaline soda lakes has not been studied in detail. Nevertheless, it cannot be ruled out that phototrophic cyanobacteria from soda lakes can implement these strategies. Soda lakes also have a number of features that potentially affect the nitrogen fixation process. For example, the presence of microbial mats with a sharp gradient of conditions creates a wide variety of ecological niches. Thus, stratified mats were described in soda lakes of Cariboo Plateau, British Columbia, Canada (Schultze-Lam et al. 1996), but this type of mats is not widely distributed in hypersaline soda lakes. Furthermore, high salinity results in lower solubility of oxygen that can be beneficial for diazotrophic bacteria (Medová et al. 2011). In addition, many representatives of anoxygenic phototrophic bacteria living on the surface sediment layer of soda lakes are also capable of nitrogen fixation (Tourova et al. 2014). The nitrogen fixation in hypersaline soda lakes attracted the attention of researchers, although the total number of publications is not high. The main evidences were obtained in Mono Lake (California) at a salinity of about 90–100 g/L. In experiments with microcosms, it was shown that a decrease in mineralization leads to an increase in the rate of nitrogen fixation. At the same time, the rate of light-dependent acetylene reduction exceeded the rate in the dark approximately threefold (Herbst 1998). Oremland (1990) further showed that the nitrogen fixation in Mono Lake was performed by different types of communities and occurred in different samples in anaerobic dark conditions or in the light with stimulation by sulfide. To our knowledge, no such data exist in the literature for hypersaline soda lakes with salinity above 100 g/L, such as, for example, the Bitter-1 lake in the Kulunda Steppe. Most interestingly, also definitely decreasing, the light-dependent acetylene reduction occurred there up to nearly soda-saturating concentrations of 350–400 g/L with the highest activity at the lowest margin during the study period (85 g/L). The maximum level of acetylene-reduction values recorded in Bitter-1 (11.19 ± 0.46 nmol C2H4/(mL h) was comparable to those registered in Mono Lake [75 ± 28 nmol C2H4/(mL h) (Oremland 1990) and 13.85–14.06 nmol C2H4/(mL h) (Herbst 1998)]. The minimal rates of acetylene reduction (0.009–1.24 nmol C2H4/(mL h) observed at salinities above 200 g/L were comparable with the rates recorded in marine sediments with low rates of nitrogen fixation (0.144 nmol C2H4/(g(dr w) h) (Herbert 1975). One of the most interesting results of this study is a very limited diversity of nifH gene during the salt-saturating period of 2011–2012 in Bitter-1 with the only detectable sequences belonging to anaerobic sulfate-reducing Deltaproteobacteria and Clostridia. In the samples from the surface layers of the sediments, we could not detect gene sequences belonging to known representatives of phototrophic microorganisms, including possibly obtained by cyanobacteria as the result of horizontal transfer from deltaproteobacteria (Bolhuis et al. 2010). The high concentration of chlorophyll a (Table 1) in these samples was possibly due to the dominance of eukaryotic alga Dunaliella sp. (Fig. 2f–f') which is not capable of nitrogen fixation. On the other hand, an earlier analysis of nifH gene in the samples from Bitter-1 lake collected at a salinity of 300 g/L in 2009 (Tourova et al. 2014) detected a presence of extremely salt-tolerant diazotrophic cyanobacteria of the genus Euhalothece and anoxygenic purple sulfur bacteria of the genus Halorhodospira. Although, at such salinity, sulfate-reducing bacteria were predicted to be inhibited due to the thermodynamic constraints of low-energy-generating catabolism (Oren 1999, 2011b), they were still detectable both by the specific molecular marker (dsrB) in situ (Foti et al. 2007, 2008) and also by cultivation approach, in particular the extremely salt-tolerant lithotrophic genera Desulfonatronospira and Desulfonatronovibrio and the acetate–propionate oxidizing genera Desulfonatronobacter and ‘Candidatus Synthrophonatronum’ (Sorokin et al. 2015a, b; Sorokin 2017). Thus, the nifH gene screening suggests that, at 350–400 g/L, the nitrogen fixation in hypersaline soda lakes is probably performed by anaerobic heterotrophs and sulfate-reducing bacteria, and at salinity lower than 300 g/L oxygenic and anoxygenic phototrophic bacteria. This conclusion was verified in experiments with phototrophic enrichment cultures run at variable salt concentrations that demonstrated activation of heterocystous diazotrophic cyanobacteria of the genus Nodularia only at low salinity and the dominance of nonheterocystous filamentous potentially diazotrophic cyanobacteria of the genera Geitlerinema and Nodosilinea at intermediate salinities of 70–150 g/L. At conditions, close to salt saturation, the only oxygenic phototroph capable of diazotrophy seems to be Euhalothece (whose capacity for nitrogen fixation is still poorly studied), while, at anaerobic conditions, the anoxygenic phototrophic bacteria of the genus Ectothiorhodospira and sulfate-reducing bacteria might still be active at low level of activity. Conclusion Communities of haloalkaliphilic bacteria from the Bitter-1 hypersaline soda lake have the ability to fix molecular nitrogen in a wide range of salinity (from 20 to 400 g/L), which can be explained by the presence of several groups of diazotrophs with significantly different salinity tolerance. The rate of nitrogen fixation depends on the salinity and can have an interannual dynamics driven by the hydrology of the lake. Sulphate reduction and nitrogen fixation rates associated with roots, rhizomes and sediments from Zostera noltii and Spartina maritima meadows Lise B. Nielsen,1 Kai Finster,1 David T. Welsh,2 Andrew Donelly,3 Rodney A. Herbert,3 Rutger de Wit4 and Bente Aa. Lomstein1* 1Department of Microbial Ecology, Institute of Biological Sciences, University of Aarhus, Building 540, Ny Munkegade, DK-8000 Aarhus, Denmark. 2Dipartimento di Scienze Ambientali, Universita degli Studi di Parma, Parco Area delle Scienze 331 A, I-43100 Parma, Italy. 3Department of Biological Sciences, University of Dundee, Dundee DD1 4HN, UK. 4Laboratoire d’Océanographie Biologique, Centre d’Océanographie et de Biologie Marine, Université Bordeaux I, CNRS-UMR 5805, 2 rue Professeur Jolyet, F-33120 Arcachon, France. Summary Sulphate reduction rates (SRR) and nitrogen fixation rates (NFR) associated with isolated roots, rhizomes and sediment from the rhizosphere of the marine macrophytes Zostera noltii and Spartina maritima, and the presence and distribution of Bacteria on the roots and rhizomes, were investigated. Between 1% and 3% of the surface area of the roots and rhizomes of both macrophytes were colonized by Bacteria. Bacteria on the surfaces of S. maritima roots and rhizomes were evenly distributed, while the distribution of Bacteria on Z. noltii roots and rhizomes was patchy. Root- and rhizome-associated SRR and NFR were always higher than rates in the bulk sediment. In particular, nitrogen fixation associated with the roots and rhizomes was 41–650-fold higher than in the bulk sediment. Despite the fact that sulphate reduction was elevated on roots and rhizomes compared with bulk sediment, the contribution of plant-associated sulphate reduction to overall sulphate reduction was small (≤ 11%). In contrast, nitrogen fixation associated with the roots and rhizomes accounted for 31% and 91% of the nitrogen fixed in the rhizosphere of Z. noltii and S. maritima respectively. In addition, plant-associated nitrogen fixation could supply 37–1613% of the nitrogen needed by the sulphate-reducing community. Sucrose stimulated nitrogen fixation and sulphate reduction significantly in the root and rhizome compartments of both macrophytes, but not in the bulk sediment. Introduction Sea grass beds and Spartina marshes are among the most productive ecosystems in shallow coastal marine environments. The rhizosphere of marine phanerogams has long been recognized as a metabolically dynamic environment in which the macro- and microbiota interact with each other (Moriarty et al., 1985; Yoch and Whiting, 1986; Moriarty and Boon, 1989; Hemminga et al., 1991; Glazebrook et al., 1996; Hines et al., 1999; Welsh, 2000). Many studies have demonstrated that rates of nitrogen fixation, sulphate reduction and overall bacterial productivity are significantly enhanced in phanerogam-bearing sediments compared with adjacent bare sediment (Moriarty et al., 1990; O’Donohue et al., 1991; Pollard and Moriarty, 1991; Holmer and Nielsen, 1996; Isaksen and Finster, 1996; Welsh et al., 1996; Hansen et al., 2000). In addition, it has been shown that these processes are coupled to the photosynthetic activity of the plants (Whiting et al., 1986; Moriarty et al., 1990, Welsh et al., 1997; Blaabjerg et al., 1998; Hines et al., 1999). Consequently, it has been proposed that microbial activity could be fuelled by a photosynthetically driven excretion of dissolved organic compounds to the rhizosphere (Penhale and Smith, 1977; Wetzel and Penhale, 1979; Moriarty et al., 1986; Welsh et al., 1997; Blaabjerg et al., 1998; Hansen et al., 2000). In a recent experiment, Boschker et al. (2000) called this coupling into question. However, these experiments were carried out with either intact cores or sediment slurries, which did not provide information on the spatial distribution of the processes and their association with roots and rhizomes. Recently, Blaabjerg and Finster (1998) demonstrated high sulphate reduction activities on isolated roots and rhizomes of the eelgrass Zostera marina, which indicated that roots and rhizomes were habitats for substantial populations of sulphate-reducing Bacteria. Further, Küsel et al. (1999) showed that sulphate-reducers colonized the rhizoplane and the deeper parts of the roots of Halodule wrightii. The rhizosphere compartments of both Z. noltii and S. maritima in Arcachon Bay, France, were examined. Z. noltii is the predominant phanerogam on the intertidal flats, while S. maritima occurs as a narrow vegetation band between the intertidal flats and the salt marshes. Sulphate-reducers are major contributors to carbon cycling in anoxic coastal marine sediments (Jørgensen, 1982) and are significant contributors to nitrogen fixation in the rhizosphere of marine macrophytes (Welsh, 2000). In this study, we report on the following investigations: (i) scanning electron microscopy of roots and rhizomes to visualize the degree of colonization and the distribution patterns of Bacteria, (ii) measurements of nitrogen fixation and sulphate reduction associated with isolated roots and rhizomes, (iii) measurements of nitrogen fixation and sulphate reduction in bulk sediment to evaluate the overall significance of the root- and rhizome-associated processes, (iv) measurements of sulphate reduction rates in intact cores of vegetated sediment to evaluate the incubation procedure in (ii) and (iii), (v) comparison of nitrogen fixation rates in the presence and absence of molybdate (a specific inhibitor of sulphate reduction) in order to determine the contribution of sulphate-reducers to the overall anaerobic nitrogen fixation in the rhizosphere, and (vi) studies of the effect of sucrose as an additional carbon and/or energy source on sulphate reduction and nitrogen fixation. Sucrose was chosen for the following reasons: (i) it has been identified as the principle and often sole transport carbohydrate in Angiosperms (Salisbury and Ross, 1992), (ii) Burke et al. (1996) demonstrated that sugars, including sucrose, are a major carbohydrate reserve in Z. marina roots and rhizomes, and (iii) Welsh et al. (1997) demonstrated that sucrose stimulated nitrogen fixation in sediments in which sulphate-reducing Bacteria were the dominant nitrogen fixers. Results Colonization of roots and rhizomes Figure 1 shows electron micrographs of Z. noltii (A and B) and S. maritima (C and D) root surfaces, and Fig. 2 shows electron micrographs of rhizome surfaces of Z. noltii (A and B) and S. maritima (C and D). There was a pronounced difference between the root tissue of the two species. Z. noltii root tissue showed great physical heterogeneity between both individual roots and distance from the rhizome. The number of root hairs and depth of longitudinal striations varied between individual roots. In contrast, S. maritima roots were more uniform and showed little or no physical variation between individual roots. The bacterial cells on Z. noltii roots were distributed in patches, while the Bacteria attached to S. maritima were more evenly distributed along the root surface. The number of Bacteria on Z. noltii roots (\(2.8 \times 10^3\) cells mm\(^{-2}\)) exceeded the number of Bacteria attached to S. maritima roots (\(1.6 \times 10^3\) cells mm\(^{-2}\)). In contrast to the root tissue, rhizome tissue samples were more homogeneous. The density of Bacteria on Z. noltii rhizomes was slightly lower (\(2.5 \times 10^3\) cells mm\(^{-2}\)) than on Z. noltii roots. On S. maritima, the Bacteria density on rhizomes (\(1.9 \times 10^3\) cells mm\(^{-2}\)) was slightly elevated compared with roots. Bacteria covered approximately 1–3% of the root and rhizome surface area given a planar average area of a bacterial cell of 1 \( \mu \)m\(^2\). Sulphate reduction in intact cores from a Z. noltii meadow Sulphate reduction rates in intact sediment cores were 1052 nmol cm\(^{-3}\) d\(^{-1}\) (SD \( \pm \) 209 nmol cm\(^{-3}\) d\(^{-1}\)) in the unamended control cores and 1623 nmol cm\(^{-3}\) d\(^{-1}\) (SD \( \pm \) 290 nmol cm\(^{-3}\) d\(^{-1}\)) in the sucrose-amended cores. The sum of the unamended sulphate reduction rates associated with the different compartments (roots, rhizomes, sediment) equalled 830 nmol SO\(_4^{2-}\) cm\(^{-3}\) d\(^{-1}\), which is in agreement with the sulphate reduction rates obtained in intact unamended cores. Sulphate and acetylene reduction rates associated with isolated roots, rhizomes and the rhizosphere sediment Root- and rhizome-associated sulphate reduction rates (SRR) exceeded SRR in the bulk sediment (Fig. 3A). SRR associated with Z. noltii and S. maritima roots were approximately 15 and four times higher than the SRR in the surrounding sediment. SRR associated with Z. noltii and S. maritima rhizomes were \( \approx \) seven and 11 times higher than the SRR in the bulk sediment. The nitrogen fixation rates (NFR) associated with roots and rhizomes of Z. noltii were 41 and 142 times higher, respectively, than the NFR in the bulk sediment, whereas the NFR associated with S. maritima roots and rhizomes exceeded sediment rates by 357–650-fold (Fig. 3B). Sulphate reduction was significantly stimulated by the addition of sucrose to the root and rhizome compartments of both macrophytes (\(P = 0.001\)), but not by the addition of sucrose to the bulk sediment (\(P = 0.064\)). In addition, nitrogen fixation was significantly stimulated by the addition of sucrose to the root and rhizome compartments (\(P = 0.0002\)), but not to the bulk sediment (\(P = 0.95\)). The inhibition of sulphate-reducing Bacteria with MoO\(_4^{2-}\) allowed us to estimate the contribution of sulphate-reducing Bacteria to the overall nitrogen fixation by the microbial community. All nitrogen fixation activity in the Z. noltii bulk sediment was owing to sulphate-reducing Bacteria. Sulphate-reducing Bacteria attached to roots and rhizomes of Z. noltii were responsible for 69% and Fig. 1. Scanning electron micrographs of Z. noltii (A and B) and S. maritima root surfaces (C and D). Bar = 0.1 mm (A and C), 2 μm (B) and 1 μm (D). 50% of the nitrogen fixing activity respectively (\( P = 0.008, P = 0.017 \)). Sulphate-reducing Bacteria attached to S. maritima rhizomes were responsible for 78% of the nitrogen fixation activity (\( P = 0.016 \)), whereas sulphate-reducing Bacteria in the bulk sediment were responsible for 59% of the total nitrogen fixation (\( P = 0.008 \)). Mean values of NFR on S. maritima roots in the absence and presence of MoO\(_4^{2-}\) differed by 30%. This difference, however, was not statistically significant (\( P = 0.14 \)), owing to large standard errors of the mean of the nitrogen fixation rates. Data presented in Fig. 3 (A and B) show the process rates associated with roots, rhizomes and bulk sediment. The quantitative importance of the three compartments (Table 1) was clearly demonstrated when the rates were normalized to volume instead of dry weight (dw). In the rhizosphere, sulphate reduction in bulk sediment accounted for \( \approx 96\% \) (Z. noltii) and 90% (S. maritima) of the overall sulphate reduction rates, respectively, while root- and rhizome-associated sulphate-reducers only contributed 4% (Z. noltii) and 11% (S. maritima), respectively, of the overall sulphate reduction rates. Considering nitrogen fixation, roots and rhizomes played a quantitatively more important role than the bulk sediment. Z. noltii roots and rhizomes accounted for about 31% of the total rhizosphere nitrogen fixation, whereas S. maritima roots and rhizomes contributed \( \approx 91\% \) of the total rhizosphere nitrogen fixation (Table 1). Discussion The presence of Bacteria on roots and rhizomes and their Fig. 2. Scanning electron micrographs of Z. noltii (A and B) and S. maritima rhizome surfaces (C and D). Bar = 0.1 mm (A and C), 5 μm (B) and 2 μm (D). distribution was investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Figs 1 and 2). This technology has proved to be a valuable tool for examining Bacteria attached to plant tissues (Paterson and Wright, 1986; Kinkel, 1997). In this experiment, SEM of S. maritima and Z. noltii samples provided quantitative data on the bacterial population that colonized the surfaces of the root and rhizome. It also allowed a qualitative assessment of the physical environment of the plant surfaces, which provided some insight into how the root structures of the plants differed as microbial habitats. Unfortunately, this method does not allow identification of the different functional Bacteria. Future investigations should therefore include molecular techniques combined with confocal laser scanning microscopy in order to obtain more detailed knowledge on the distribution of the different functional bacterial populations on the rhizoplane. In a previous study, McClung et al. (1983) found that nitrogen-fixing Bacteria were present both at the rhizoplane and inside the root tissue using most probable number (MPN) counts and transmission electron microscopy. Further, Küsel et al. (1999) showed, by use of \(^{33}\)P-labelled probes, that sulphate-reducers colonized the rhizoplane as well as the deeper parts of roots of the sea grass H. wrightii. The agreement between the SRR determined in intact cores and the sum of SRR associated with roots, rhizomes and bulk sediment demonstrated that the sample preparation and incubation procedure did not influence the bacterial activities. The high sulphate and acetylene reduction rates associated with isolated roots and rhizomes indicated that both of these rhizosphere compartments served as important habitats for sulphate-reducing and nitrogen-fixing Fig. 3. Sulphate reduction rates (A) and nitrogen fixation rates (B) within the three-rhizosphere compartments: roots, rhizomes and bulk sediment of the macrophytes Z. noltii and S. maritima. Rates are given in nmol gdw\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\). Bacteria (Fig. 3A and B). Previously, Hines et al. (1999), using nucleic acid probes, demonstrated that rRNA from sulphate-reducing Bacteria accounted for 43% of the RNA from members of the domain Bacteria in sediments of a S. alterniflora marsh. In addition, they showed that the highest percentages of sulphate-reducing Bacteria were physically associated with the surfaces of S. alterniflora roots. The dramatic difference between rates associated with roots and rhizomes, and bulk sediment, respectively, may be a result of differences in the size of the active microbial populations. The size of the sulphate-reducing community can be estimated from community SRR and rates determined for single cells, assuming that all cells had been equally active. The per cell sulphate reduction rate of \(4.2 \times 10^{-15}\) mol sulphate cell\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) was derived from the literature (Vester and Ingvorsen, 1998). By dividing the community rates determined in our experiments with the per cell value given above, we estimate that root- and rhizome-associated populations of sulphate-reducers were \(10^7 - 10^8\) cells gdw\(^{-1}\) of root or rhizome tissue and the sediment populations were \(10^6 - 10^7\) cells g\(^{-1}\) dry 68 L. Sulphate reduction and nitrogen fixation rates are normalized to volume of roots, rhizomes or sediment. In addition, the population size of the bulk sediment agrees with previously reported numbers obtained by MPN enumerations of sulphate-reducers in sediment from the same sampling station (Welsh et al., 1996). The estimated size of the root- and rhizome-associated populations of sulphate-reducers is one order of magnitude higher than the size of the sediment population on a dry weight basis. This difference explains the differences in SRR between the two compartments. The number of sulphate-reducers estimated from the SRR is within the same order of magnitude as the total cell numbers determined from SEM data (2 × 108 cells gdw−1 on Z. noltii; 2 × 107 cells gdw−1 on S. maritima). The total number of Bacteria on the rhizoplane of S. alterniflora (≈2 × 108 cells gdw−1) that was determined by McClung et al. (1983) was similar to our estimates. However, inspection of SEM micrographs indicated that SEM-based cell numbers may underestimate the true population size owing to the patchiness in distribution of cells and the inability of the method to quantify the colonization inside roots and rhizomes. The significance of root- and rhizome-associated processes and the nitrogen supply by nitrogen fixation The fraction of nitrogen demand by sulphate-reducers that could be met by their ability to fix nitrogen was estimated by use of a set of equations formulated by Blackburn (1983) for non-steady state conditions: (i) Co = 2Sr (ii) i = Co × Nc × E/(1 − E), in which Co = carbon oxidation rate, Sr = sulphate reduction rate, i = nitrogen incorporation rate, Nc = nitrogen to carbon content of Bacteria cells (≈0.2; Fagerbakke et al., 1996) and E = efficiency of carbon incorporation (≈0.06; Hill, 1976). The results of these estimates are presented in Table 1. Nitrogen fixation could supply 37–1613% of the N requirements of sulphate-reducers associated with roots and rhizomes, and < 18% of the nitrogen requirement of sulphate-reducers in the bulk sediment. Consequently, root- and rhizome-associated sulphate-reducers may be a significant source of nitrogen to the rhizosphere community, including the plants. Fixed nitrogen may have been transferred directly to the plant as NH4+, as demonstrated by O’Donohue et al. (1991). They found that 50% of the total 15N2 fixed was present in the above-ground biomass of Z. capricorni after 6 h of incubation. Alternatively, the fixed nitrogen may have been available when the Bacteria died and the cell components were mineralized. Despite the fact that there were high rates of sulphate reduction associated with the isolated roots and rhizomes, their contribution to the total sulphate reduction in intact sediments was of minor importance (4% in Z. noltii, 11% in S. maritima). These values are consistent with estimates reported by Hansen et al. (2000). They found that approximately 4% of the sulphate reduction was associated with roots and rhizomes of the seagrass Z. capricorni. In both studies, this can mainly be attributed to the relative small volume of roots and rhizomes compared with the bulk sediment. In contrast, nitrogen fixation associated with roots and rhizomes accounted for a significant proportion of the total nitrogen fixed (31% in Z. noltii and 91% in S. maritima). Hansen et al. (2000) reported that 17% of the integrated sediment nitrogen fixation accomplished by anaerobic Bacteria was associated with the roots and rhizomes. The low nitrogen fixation rates in the bulk sediment compared with the rates associated with roots and rhizomes may be owing to a sufficient supply of ammonium in bulk sediment from other sources. It can be anticipated that the supply of ammonium would inhibit nitrogen fixation, as was demonstrated for S. alterniflora- and Z. capricorni–vegetated sediments (Yoch and Whiting, 1986; Hansen et al., 2000). The surplus of nitrogen fixed by the root-associated sulphate-reducing Bacteria may have meant that the sulphate-reducers supplied nitrogen for the plant. The energy for this highly costly process may have been supplied by the plant host in the form of soluble exudates, e.g. sucrose. This hypothesis is supported by numerous investigations (Wetzel and Penhale, 1979; Moriarty et al., 1990; O’Donohue et al., 1991; Pollard and Moriarty, 1991; Welsh et al., 1996; Blaabjerg et al., 1998; Hansen et al., 2000). For example, Wetzel and Penhale (1979) demonstrated that dissolved organic carbon was released from the roots of the seagrasses Z. marina, Thalassia testudinum and Halodule wrightii using [14C]-NaHCO3 added to the water column. By use of mass balance calculations Hansen et al. (2000) estimated that 8–18% of the carbon fixed by the sea grass Z. capricorni was released to the rhizosphere by the root system. The immediate and significant stimulation of the root- and rhizome-associated SRR after the addition of sucrose indicated that the community of sulphate-reducers was preadapted to this energy and/or carbon source or to the fermentation products generated from the degradation of sucrose by other members of the microbial community. The results of this study add to the growing body of evidence that there is a specific relationship between sulphate-reducing Bacteria and the below-ground tissue of marine macrophytes. This relationship may be based on the reciprocal exchange of fixed carbon and nitrogen between the plants and Bacteria. Thus, sulphate-reducers, in addition to being key-players in carbon cycling in the rhizosphere of marine angiosperms, may also be implicitly involved in nitrogen cycling and thereby constitute an energy shunt between the two cycles. Experimental procedures Sampling site and procedure Sediment samples were collected within a large intertidal seagrass meadow of Z. noltii situated on the Île aux Oiseaux in the central part of the Bay of Arcachon and stands of S. maritima situated in the inner part of the Bay of Arcachon, France. See Caumette et al. (1996) for a detailed description of the Bay of Arcachon. Sampling was carried out using PVC cores (19 cm i.d., length 20 cm) between June 25 and July 5, 1997 (Z. noltii meadow) and 1998 (S. maritima stands). The cores were stored in a mesocosm that was continuously flushed with seawater. The temperature was kept at the in situ temperature and the light conditions were seminatural, as previously described in Welsh et al. (1997). Sediment characteristics Sediment density (g cm\(^{-3}\)) was determined from the fresh weight of 2 ml of sediment (\(n = 10\)). Sediment water content (g of water g\(^{-1}\) porewater + sediment) was determined as the weight loss after drying at 105\(^\circ\)C for 24 h (\(n = 10\)). Data on sediment characteristics are given in Table 2. The average root and rhizome biomass in the upper 3 cm of the Z. noltii bed and the upper 12 cm of the S. maritima sediment was determined as the biomass of live roots and rhizomes from 850 cm\(^3\) of Z. noltii and 3400 cm\(^3\) of S. maritima sediment. Porewater sulphate concentrations were determined as described in Isaksen and Finster (1996). Sample preparation and incubation condition The upper 3 cm of the sediment vegetated with Z. noltii and the upper 12 cm of the sediment vegetated with S. maritima were separated into the following three fractions: (i) live roots, (ii) live rhizomes, and (iii) bulk sediment without roots and rhizomes. Roots and rhizomes were obtained by washing the sediment in running seawater. Recent studies by Blaabjerg and Finster (1998) showed that the activity of sulphate-reducers, which were associated with the roots of Z. marina, was not affected after exposure to air for 8 h. A prolonged exposure of the roots and rhizomes to oxygen was avoided by storage in oxygen-free seawater prior to transfer to a glove bag with a N\(_2\) atmosphere. Live roots and rhizomes were identified by colour, structure and texture. Bulk sediment was obtained by removing plant material from mixed sediment samples with a pair of forceps. Removal of plant material from the sediment was carried out under a N\(_2\) atmosphere. Measurements of root- and rhizome-associated sulphate reduction were carried out in 10 ml Labco exetainers filled with 5 ml of 0.2 \( \mu \)m of filtered seawater. Nitrogen fixation associated with roots and rhizomes was measured in 13 ml venoject tubes (TERUMO) filled with 3 ml of 0.2 \( \mu \)m of filtered seawater. The seawater was collected close to the sampling site. Roots or rhizomes (\(~30\) mg dw incubation\(^{-1}\)) were transferred to the prepared containers. Homogenized bulk sediment was transferred to preweighted containers using a plastic syringe with the luer tip removed: 1 ml of sediment for sulphate reduction was transferred to 5 ml Labco exetainers and 3 ml of sediment for nitrogen fixation were transferred to 13 ml venoject tubes (TERUMO). The headspace of the containers was exchanged with nitrogen gas after sample addition to ensure anoxia during the incubation. Incubations were performed in four or five replicates. Sucrose and molybdate were added from sterile stock solutions with a syringe through the rubber septum prior to sample addition. The final concentrations were 2 mmol C l\(^{-1}\) and 20 mmol MoO\(_4^{2-}\) l\(^{-1}\) respectively. Electron microscopy Samples were fixed in 2.5% (w/v) gluteraldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 6.8) for 48 h and rinsed in phosphate buffer before complete dehydration of the samples by passing them through an ascending ethanol–acetone series, followed by critically point drying using the Polaron E3000 Series II critical point drying apparatus. Specimens were then mounted on aluminum stubs using double-sided carbon tabs and coated for 5 min using a Polaron E5100 Series II cool sputter coater fitted with an Au–Pd target. Specimens were stored in a desiccator prior to viewing in a JEOL JSM-35 scanning electron microscope. The accelerating voltage was 15 kV. Quantitative data on bacterial colonization were obtained by counting cells in 100 fields of 500 \( \mu \)m\(^2\). Sulphate and acetylene reduction rate measurements The sulphate reduction rate measurements were initiated by injection of 10 \( \mu \)l of \( ^{35} \)SO\(_4^{2-}\) tracer dissolved in filtered seawater (final activity \( \approx 50 \) kBq ml\(^{-1}\)). The tubes were shaken vigorously and incubated for 8 h at 20°C in the dark. Incubations of roots and rhizomes were stopped by the direct injection of 1 ml 20% (w/v) Zn–acetate into the incubation vessels. Sediment samples received 2 ml of Zn–acetate. Prior to H\(_2^{35}\)S and \( ^{35} \)SO\(_4^{2-}\) measurements, the roots and rhizomes were removed from the samples and dried at 105°C for 24 h for biomass dry weight determination. After weighing, roots and rhizomes were distilled together with their respective samples. The production of H\(_2^{35}\)S was determined by the one-step Cr\(^{2+}\) distillation method (Fossing and Jørgensen, 1989) and calculations were performed as described by Isaksen and Finster (1996). Incubations of intact sediment cores (\( n = 3 \)) from the Z. noltii meadow were carried out to evaluate the effect of the sediment handling when obtaining material for the rate measurements in the different compartments. Intact cores (inner diameter 3.6 cm) were injected with anoxic seawater supplemented with sucrose into the upper 3 cm layer of the sediment prior to \( ^{35} \)SO\(_4^{2-}\) tracer addition (final activity \( \approx 50 \) kBq ml\(^{-1}\)) through silicone rubber-filled injection ports in the tube wall. The resultant final porewater concentration of sucrose was 0.2 mM. The upper 3 cm of the sediment corresponded to the extension of the rhizosphere in the sediment. Cores injected with anoxic seawater served as controls. The cores were incubated for 8 h at 20°C in the dark. The incubations were stopped by transferring the upper 3 cm of sediment to plastic centrifuge tubes that contained 10 ml of 20% (w/v) Zn–acetate. After transfer, the tubes were sealed with a plastic lid and shaken vigorously. The samples were frozen until further processing and analysis as described above. Acetylene reduction determinations were initiated by injecting acetylene into the tubes to a final concentration of 10% in the headspace. Tubes were vigorously shaken and incubated at 20°C for 8 h. Incubations were stopped by injection of 1 ml of trichloroacetic acid and the suspension was vigorously mixed. Ethylene concentrations were determined by gas chromatography, as described by Welsh et al. (1996). Acetylene reduction rates were also determined in the presence of MoO\(_4^{2-}\), a specific inhibitor of sulphate-reducing Bacteria. Thus, the contribution of sulphate-reducers to the overall nitrogen fixation in the different compartments could be estimated by subtracting nitrogen fixation rates measured in the presence of MoO\(_4^{2-}\) from rates determined in its absence. Statistical analysis The data for sulphate reduction rates and nitrogen fixation rates associated with either sediment or roots and rhizomes were analysed separately. Treatment effects were, in principle, analysed using a conventional two-way model I ANOVA with the presence or absence of sucrose as one fixed factor and the rhizosphere fraction as the other fixed factor. The effect of molybdate was analysed individually for each of the six compartments (Z. noltii roots, rhizomes and bulk sediment, and S. maritima roots, rhizomes and bulk sediment) using a conventional one-way model I ANOVA with the presence or absence of molybdate as the fixed factor. The significance levels were obtained using the observed \( F \)-value plus 9999 \( F \)-values generated by random allocations of the data as a distribution of the F-statistics specific for each set of data (Manly, 1996). The distributions of the F-statistics were performed using the software package RT v.2.1.TRIAL on the original data. In all cases, the results of the ANOVA test gave the same result as if the F-table was used. Nitrogen Fixation in Sediments and the Rhizosphere of the Seagrass Zostera capricorni M. J. O'Donohue,1 D. J. W. Moriarty,2 and I. C. Mac Rae1 1Department of Microbiology, University of Queensland, St. Lucia, Queensland 4072; and 2CSIRO Marine Laboratories, P.O. Box 120, Cleveland, Queensland 4163, Australia Received: November 19, 1990; Revised: March 19, 1991 Abstract. Rates of nitrogen fixation in seagrass beds (Zostera capricorni) were determined with \(^{15}\)N and reduction of acetylene in intact cores of sediment and seagrass. There was good agreement in the results from the two techniques, with a molar ratio of 3 : 1.9 ethylene : ammonia produced. Fixed nitrogen was rapidly utilized by the plants, with significant amounts of \(^{15}\)N found in the roots and rhizomes and 50% of fixed \(^{15}\)N apparently translocated to the leaves. Rates of fixation were high in summer (25 to 40 mg N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) and lower in winter (10 mg N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) and were estimated to supply between one-third and one-half of the nitrogen requirements of the seagrass. Rates of nitrogen fixation were greater in the light than in the dark, and in cores of intact seagrass than in defoliated cores, indicating that the bacteria were dependent on organic compounds secreted by the plants. Introduction Seagrass communities are some of the most productive of all the shallow coastal environments [14]. To sustain high growth rates the seagrasses require large amounts of inorganic nitrogen and phosphorus [20]. The concentrations of inorganic nitrogenous nutrients, particularly ammonia, in interstitial water in seagrass beds may not be sufficient to meet the short-term growth requirements of the seagrass [16, 20]. In shallow benthic environments, fixation of gaseous dinitrogen, which will be referred to below as nitrogen fixation, is the major source of nitrogen for plants and microorganisms [6]. Nitrogen fixation by microorganisms occurs in the phyllosphere and rhizosphere of the seagrasses [7–9, 21, 24, 25]. Studies on seagrass productivities and nitrogen cycling on Moreton Bay, Queensland, indicate that there is a discrepancy between the available nitrogen and the nitrogen requirements of the seagrass [16]. The research described here was undertaken to determine whether nitrogen fixation was an important pro- Offprint requests to: D. J. W. Moriarty. cess contributing to the nitrogen requirements of the seagrasses of Moreton Bay. Our aims were to determine the rates of nitrogen fixation in undisturbed cores of sediment and to investigate interactions of seagrass photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation in the rhizosphere. The interactions of seagrass and bacteria were investigated by measuring rates of acetylene reduction in light and dark studies, the effect of defoliation of seagrass stands on nitrogen fixation in the sediments, and fixation of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) in the rhizosphere. Rates of acetylene reduction have been used to estimate nitrogenase activity in the seagrass beds because they are simple to apply, but as acetylene is not a natural substrate of nitrogenase, they are indirect and may be inaccurate. Therefore, we compared the rates of nitrogen fixation, measured with the acetylene reduction technique, with rates of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) fixation. Constraints upon the use of this stable isotope in short-term experiments, such as the speed at which it diffuses to the nitrogen fixation sites and lengthy analyses, can be overcome with the use of the easily manipulated intact core and the perfusion technique described by O'Donohue et al. [19]. Materials and Methods Study Site Two sample sites in Moreton Bay, Queensland, Australia (27°38'S, 153°25'E) were selected for study. The sites used in this study were Amity (Wanga Wallen) Banks off the northern tip of North Stradbroke Island (containing Zostera capricorni (Aschers.) and Cymodocea serrulata) and Pelican Banks on the mainland side of North Stradbroke Island (containing Zostera capricorni). Two morphological types of Zostera capricorni were present. Long-leaf Z. capricorni (leaf length of 200 to 300 mm; width of approximately 5 mm) was generally found in the subtidal areas while the short-leaf form (20 to 40 mm long and 1 to 2 mm wide) predominated in the intertidal regions. The greatest root and rhizome density is found in the top 4 cm of the seagrass beds in both morphological forms [1]. The sediment consists of mainly sand with a low silt/clay and organic carbon content [1]. Cores from the seagrass bed, containing seagrasses and sediment, were collected with polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipe of 15 or 10 cm diameter and 15 cm long with one end sharpened to cut through roots and rhizomes [19]. The cores were transported in bins of seawater and were stored in shaded fiber glass holding tanks. Acetylene Reduction Rates of acetylene reduction were measured in intact cores of seagrass sediment with two different techniques. First, a perfusion method: Acrylic chambers were attached to the top of the cores and filled with seawater containing acetylene (20% v/v). A plug was removed from a hole in the base of the cores, and the acetylenated water perfused slowly through the sediment. Second, a lacunal diffusion method: Seawater containing acetylene was placed in acrylic chambers attached to the cores and the acetylene diffused through the seagrass lacunae to the rhizosphere. For both techniques, samples of interstitial water were collected from various sediment depths and analyzed for acetylene and ethylene by gas chromatography. The methods were described in detail by O'Donohue et al. [19]. For some experiments, acetylene reduction was also measured in glass jars [19]. The effect of light and dark incubation of seagrass on acetylene reduction activity was determined in cores that were preincubated in the dark for 12 hours. Seasonal Variation and the Effects of Defoliation Seasonal rates and the effects of defoliation on acetylene reduction activity in short-leaf Zostera capricorni beds were determined by perfusion analyses between May 1986 and April 1987 and in December 1987. Perforated PVC tubes 15 cm long and 10.5 cm in diameter were prepared by cutting many holes (2 cm diameter) in the sides to allow interstitial water exchange. These cores were numbered and placed in sequence into the seagrass beds in two rows. One set of cores was put into position at the start of winter in May 1986. The seagrass leaves in the cores were cut off and regrowth was removed each fortnight thereafter, until it stopped. A second set of cores was put in place for summer experiments in January 1987. All the seagrass leaves were removed from within the cores, and shade cloth was placed over the cores to prevent regrowth. For each experiment, three of the numbered PVC tubes were selected from within the defoliated (decomposition) zone, and cores were collected after the perforated PVC tubing was replaced by 18-cm-long flanged PVC pipes of the same diameter. For comparison with the defoliated cores, three cores were also collected from nearby stands of seagrass (normal seagrass cores). In both the winter and the summer experiments the first cores to be analyzed were collected on the day the seagrass leaves were removed. Perfusion analyses of acetylene reduction activity were performed for 6 hours, with samples of interstitial water being collected at 0, 2, 4, and 6 hours at depths 2, 6, 10, and 14 cm. Three bare sediment cores from a sand bank adjacent to the sample site on Pelican Banks were collected in May 1986 and April 1987. These cores were analyzed for acetylene reduction activity using perfusion analysis. Samples were collected at the depths and times outlined for the seagrass and defoliated cores. Comparison of Acetylene Reduction and \(^{15}N_2\) Fixation Six cores from short-leaf Zostera capricorni beds were collected from Pelican Banks in December 1986, and nitrogenase analyses were started within 24 hours. The cores were randomly divided into 2 sets of 3 cores. Acetylene reduction activity in the cores was determined using one set, while nitrogen fixation was determined using the other set. Acetylene reduction activity was determined with the perfusion method as previously described for short-leaf Zostera cores [19]. The cores were perfused with acetylenated seawater for 30 min, after which the acetylenated water was removed from the perspex chambers and replaced with normal seawater. The cores were incubated under saturating light conditions in glass tanks filled with seawater. Duplicate samples of interstitial water and the water column were collected at the start of the experiment and after 6 hours. The interstitial water was collected from the 2, 6, and 10 cm depths of the sediment. All samples were stored in 5 ml vacutainers with 50 \( \mu l \) of a 20% trichloroacetic acid (TCA) solution. The root and rhizome material was freeze-dried and weighed. The water samples were analyzed for acetylene and ethylene as previously described [19]. For the \(^{15}N_2\) analyses, cores were perfused with seawater saturated with \(^{15}N_2\) as follows. Glass bottles (4 liter capacity) containing 3.5 liters of seawater were placed on magnetic stirrers. Rubber stoppers, each holding 2 glass stopcocks, were used to seal the bottles. A vacuum pump was attached via one of the stopcocks and the other was attached to a 10 cm piece of silicone tubing sealed at the other end. The seawater was degassed for 1 hour while being vigorously stirred, and then 105 ml of \(^{15}N_2\) gas (minimum 95 atom percentage excess) was added to the evacuated bottle by injecting the gas through the silicon tubing. High purity helium gas was injected into the bottle until the pressure was equal to atmospheric pressure. The contents of the bottle were then continuously stirred for 12 hours. The \(^{15}N_2\) saturated water was then poured into the acrylic chambers attached to the top of the intact cores of seagrass and sediment and perfused through the cores for 1 hour. The chamber over the cores was refilled with seawater saturated with \(^{15}N_2\). The chambers were sealed and incubated as described for the cores used for acetylene reduction analysis. Duplicate samples of 400 \( \mu l \) of interstitial and water column water were collected initially and after 6 hours, and stored with 20% TCA in 5 ml vacutainers. At the end of the analyses the seagrass leaves were removed from the plants at the sediment surface and the cores were extruded from the PVC pipe. The leaves were stored in plastic bags at \(-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). The sediment core was bisected and each half sectioned into 0–4, 4–8, and 8–12 cm fractions. Each of the sections was immediately placed into a plastic bag with 50 ml of 4% TCA in deionized water, and then sealed and mixed to stop bacterial activity. One half of the core was then stored at \(-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). The core sections were sieved through a 3 mm nylon mesh into a small plastic bucket. The sediment and the water from the washing were collected and placed into plastic bags and freeze-dried. The remaining plant material with adhering sediment was thoroughly washed in 50 ml of 2% TCA in deionized water to remove the closely-adhering sediment. The sediment was placed with the rinse water into plastic bags and freeze-dried. The clean plant material was also freeze-dried. As a control, a fourth seagrass core was treated as described above except that it was perfused with seawater having the natural abundance of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\). Sample Analyses The interstitial and water column water samples of 400 \( \mu l \) in the vacutainers were brought to atmospheric pressure by inserting a hyperdermic needle through the rubber cap and then frozen in liquid nitrogen to eliminate water vapor. To equalize pressure in the container to that of the atmosphere, 1 ml of air was injected into the vacutainer and the contents were mixed by pumping the syringe plunger several times. A 1 ml sample was then withdrawn and injected into the mass spectrometer. Atomic ratios for N 28, 29, and 30 were determined. The natural abundance of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) was subtracted from all values. The percentage of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) excess in the water samples was obtained from the equation: \[ \text{percentage }^{15}\mathrm{N} \text{ excess} = 100 \times \left( \text{me29} + 3 \times \text{me30} \right) / 2 \times \left( \text{me28} + \text{me29} + \text{me30} \right) \] The majority of the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) was in the gas phase of vacutainer above the water sample. (The ratio of liquid to gas volume in the vacutainer was 1 : 11.5, and nitrogen is only sparingly soluble in seawater: 10.3 mg liter\(^{-1}\) at 25\(^\circ\)C). The amount of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) in the original 400 \( \mu l \) of seawater was used to determine the percentage of the total nitrogen fixed during the 6 hour analysis. Sediment, root/rhizome, and leaf samples were ground to a homogeneous mixture, digested, and analyzed for total nitrogen using the salicylic acid modification of the Kjeldahl technique for \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) by mass spectrometry [3]. Using the percentage excess per sample, rates of fixation were determined for each sample section, leaf, root and rhizome, sediment from close to the roots and rhizomes, and sediment not closely associated with the roots and rhizomes from each of the 4 cm sediment depth sections. The total N\(_2\) fixation was calculated by adjusting for the percentage excess of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) in the interstitial water and water column samples. Epiphytic Cyanobacteria Fragments of the leaves of the seagrass used in the acetylene reduction analyses were examined for epiphytic cover using fluorescence microscopy [15]. Analysis of Carbon Dioxide in the Water Column To ensure that the CO\(_2\) concentration in the seawater in the chamber during the period of the experiment was sufficient for photosynthesis, 3 ml samples of the seawater containing \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) were collected at the start of the analyses and at the end of the incubation period. Samples were analyzed for CO\(_2\) by the method of Roberts and Smith [23]. Little change was found in CO\(_2\) concentration. Nitrogen Fixation in Zostera capricorni 57 **Results** Rates of acetylene reduction were much greater in sediment slurries that were incubated anaerobically than aerobically (Table 1). There was a noticeable degree of acetylene reduction in washed roots and rhizomes and the rates in this case were faster in aerobic incubations (Table 1). No ethylene was produced from leaves incubated separately. A comparison of rates of acetylene reduction in sediments with *Zostera capricorni*, defoliated plants, and bare sand patches near the seagrass indicated that nitrogen-fixing bacteria were most active in association with organic matter from plants (Table 2). Rates of acetylene reduction were significantly faster in summer than winter (analysis of variance, $P < 0.001, F = 65.7, \text{df} = 1$). Rates were slower within each season in sediments containing defoliated rhizomes and roots than normal seagrass ($P < 0.001, F = 15.3, \text{df} = 1$). Values are amounts of nitrogen fixed for 15N fixation, and ethylene produced for acetylene reduction (means ± SE; n = 3) Discussion Seagrass beds are considered to be significant sites for nitrogen fixation in coastal areas, and to a large extent, this conclusion is based on results of experiments with acetylene as a substrate for the nitrogenase [6, 10, 21]. In order to quantify the contribution of nitrogen fixation to nitrogen cycle budgets in the field, the rates of acetylene reduction must be accurately converted to the rates of nitrogen fixation occurring under natural conditions in the field. The work reported here shows that with appropriate experimental procedures, acetylene reduction does give valid estimates of actual rates of nitrogen fixation. The rates measured with both techniques agreed well with the expected molar ratio of 3 : 2 (Table 4). Values for atom percentage excess of 15N in the plant and rhizosphere sediment were high relative to the control after only 6 hours incubation. This time period is short enough (at the ambient temperature of 25°C) to minimize effects due to disturbance caused by collection of cores and experimental manipulation [19]. Thus, the positions of bacteria in the plants, rhizosphere, and roots and the gradients of oxygen and nutrients were not radically affected. The sediment was perfused for only a short time, generally 45 min, and not continuously during the experiment. Thus, gradients of oxygen diffusing from the sediment surface and roots and rhizomes would be rapidly reestablished. Nitrogen Fixation in Zostera capricorni 61
